proof:
# Simultaneous sharp centroid-loss equality forces the opposite simplex

This is an equality classification for the ordinary cap-loss lemma.
It supplies strictness in a small-body regime, not a quantitative
stability bound or a complete mixed-integer argument.

Let d>=1, m=d+1, and let v_0,...,v_d span R^d with sole linear
dependence sum_i v_i=0. Put

    T={x:v_i.x<=1 for every i}.

Let A be a full-dimensional convex body, with every cut v_i.x=-1
proper. Write a=|A|, U_i=|A intersect {v_i.x>=-1}|, and L_i(g_A)
for its cap-loss derivative under contraction about its actual centroid.
Suppose equality holds in EVERY inequality

    L_i(g_A)>=[d^2/(d+1)] a^(1/d) U_i^((d-1)/d).             (1)

Then A is a simplex of the form

    A={x:v_i.x>=ell_i for every i},  ell_i=min_A v_i.x<-1.   (2)

Consequently -T is contained in int A and a>|T|. In particular, if
a<=|T|, every strictly positive weighted sum of (1) is STRICT.
No lower bound on the size of that strict surplus is asserted.

## 1. Equality in one direction gives an actual pyramid

For completeness, the equality argument proved in
`unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)` is included.
Shift the proper cut to scalar height0. In the notation of
`candidate 268d75cf9619baac`, its survival function F
is bounded above by

    G(t)=min{a,U(1-t/D)_+^d},
    D=dU/sigma, s=(a/U)^(1/d)>1.

The exact profile-deficit identity makes equality in (1) equivalent to
integral_R(G-F)=0. The functions are continuous and G-F>=0, hence
F=G everywhere. Positivity of every proper section identifies the
two actual support heights as t_0=D(1-s) and D.

Take an actual point p at height D. For 0<r<1, convexity gives

    p+r(A-p) subset A intersect {t>=D+r(t_0-D)}=:C_r.

Both bodies have volume r^d a, by the exact profile G. Inclusion of
full-dimensional compact convex bodies of equal volume is equality.
Indeed, if the larger had a point outside the smaller, its convex
hull with an interior ball of the smaller would contain positive
volume outside the smaller. Thus C_r=p+r(A-p).

The maximum support face is in every C_r, whose diameter tends to0
with r. It is therefore the singleton p. For x in A other than p,
set r=(D-t(x))/(D-t_0)>0. If r=1, x itself lies in the minimum
support face. If 0<r<1, the equality of caps expresses x=p+r(z-p)
for some z in A, and its height forces t(z)=t_0. Thus A is precisely
the convex hull of its unique top point and its minimum support face.
That base face has dimension d-1 because A has interior. This proof
also applies to an interval when d=1.

Apply this conclusion to each normal v_i. There are unique top points
p_i and base faces F_i={x in A:v_i.x=ell_i}, with

    A=conv({p_i} union F_i).                              (3)

## 2. The pyramid tips are distinct

For d>=2, two distinct normals v_i,v_j are linearly independent;
otherwise the sole dependence of the full family would have a zero
coefficient. If their tips were the same p, every extreme point of A
other than p would lie in F_i intersect F_j, of affine dimension at
most d-2. One may avoid invoking any extreme-point representation as
follows. For any exposed face of A not containing p, (3) places that
face in both F_i and F_j: a maximizing linear functional with value
strictly above its value at p cannot use p in its convex combination.
If A were not contained in conv({p} union (F_i intersect F_j)),
strict separation of a point from this compact convex set would give
just such a maximizing face outside it, a contradiction. The claimed
containment has affine dimension at most d-1, impossible for A.
Hence the p_i are distinct. In dimension1 the two normals are opposite,
and the unique maximum and minimum points of a nondegenerate interval
are distinct directly.

Each p_j is an extreme point of A, since it uniquely maximizes v_j.
For j!=i, equation (3) and p_j!=p_i imply p_j in F_i: otherwise its
representation would be a nontrivial convex combination of two
distinct points of A. Therefore

    v_i.p_j=ell_i for j!=i,
    v_i.p_i>ell_i.                                      (4)

## 3. No other points are needed

Suppose A were not the convex hull P of the finitely many p_i. Strict
separation supplies a linear functional whose maximum on A exceeds
its maximum on P. Its nonempty maximum face contains no p_i. Applying
(3) for every i puts this face in every F_i. This is impossible:
such a point would satisfy 0=sum_i v_i.x=sum_i ell_i, whereas every
ell_i<-1. Hence A=P.

The d+1 points are affinely independent because their hull has interior.
Their facet hyperplanes in (4) are exactly v_i.x=ell_i. Their simplex
therefore has the halfspace description (2). This can also be checked
directly: for L=-sum_i ell_i>0, the affine coordinates

    beta_i(x)=(v_i.x-ell_i)/L

sum to1. Equation (4) makes beta_i(p_j)=delta_ij, since summing (4)
over i at p_j gives v_j.p_j-ell_j=L. Thus beta_i>=0 describes exactly
their simplex.

If x in -T, then v_i.x>=-1>ell_i for every i. All its barycentric
coordinates in this simplex are strictly positive, so -T is contained
in int A. A has strictly larger d-volume. Finally each difference in
(1) is nonnegative; a positive weighted sum could be zero only if
every one were zero. This proves the stated strictness when a<=|T|.

## Scope of the strictness

The proper-A/zero-B canonical mixed-fiber branch has B subset T and
a<b/6, or in its more restricted two-residual subcase a<b/32. Hence
it cannot attain simultaneous equality in (1). This fact does NOT
show that its weighted square-root sum reaches the sufficient1/3
threshold, and does not quantify enough surplus when that threshold
fails. Replacing this strictness by an unproved uniform gap would be
an invalid final step.
